idiom_name: Thread.new + Thread::Queue#push/pop (or Thread#value for a blocking join)
implementation_notes: The stdlib gives threads and a thread-safe queue: the start method spawns a Thread and returns, the worker pushes [status, payload] onto a Thread::Queue when it finishes, and the consumer pops it (blocking only when it chooses to) - completion is a queued message rather than a callback registry. Thread#value offers the same result-later semantics but blocks the caller, and reactor gems go further; the queue form is the honest default because it needs no dependency and keeps delivery explicit. CPU-bound work still needs processes or Ractors, since the GVL serialises Ruby threads.
code_sketch:
def start_report(queue)                     # start now, returns immediately
  Thread.new do
    queue << [:ok, build_report]            # result later, via the queue
  rescue => e
    queue << [:error, e]                    # exactly one message per call
  end
end
# consumer: status, payload = queue.pop     # blocks only here
pitfalls: An exception in a Thread is swallowed unless Thread.abort_on_exception or report_on_exception is enabled - the completion then simply never arrives.
The GVL serialises CPU work: threads help with blocking I/O, not with CPU-bound operations (use processes/Ractors for those).
One queue/thread per call must be reaped and must not be shared between operations, or completions get attributed to the wrong request and threads leak.

variants.name: Async reactor on non-blocking fibers (Fiber scheduler)
variants.idiom_name: Async { } tasks on the reactor (Async::Task#wait as the completion point), or Fiber.schedule with an installed Fiber scheduler
variants.implementation_notes: The reactor realization: Async provides 'a composable asynchronous I/O framework for Ruby based on io-event', running tasks on fibers so a start call schedules work and its completion runs as a callback/continuation when the awaited I/O finishes - the historical EventMachine filled the same role. Ruby 3.0 added non-blocking fibers and a Fiber scheduler, which brings this style into the core and makes it the scalable alternative to one thread per operation. Blocking calls inside a reactor task stall every other task, so use the framework's async I/O primitives.
variants.code_sketch:
Async do                                       # reactor task, returns immediately
  task = Async { build_report }                 # start now
  report = task.wait                            # completion: yields to the reactor
  publish(report)
end
pitfalls: Reactor callbacks run on the reactor's thread: a blocking call there stalls every other task - use the framework's async I/O or hand blocking work to a thread pool.
Fiber-based completion needs the fiber scheduler (Ruby 3.0+) to be installed; mixing plain threads with reactor tasks reintroduces the synchronisation the reactor was avoiding.
